intro: Karate and taekwondo are often mixed up on signs and in movies. They have separate histories. Karate grew on Okinawa, in the old Ryukyu Kingdom, with ideas from China. Taekwondo was built in South Korea after 1945, with a new national name.

Both arts moved from small rooms into schools, armies, universities and world federations. Wars, empires and the Olympic Games shaped them. In this unit you will follow each art from its first teachers to its first Olympic medals.
By the end, you will be able to explain where each art came from and name the people who carried it. You will also compare how karate and taekwondo got their names, ranks and rule books.
bigQuestion: How did karate and taekwondo each become an art with a national name, a school plan and a world federation?

title: Okinawa and Korea

chapters.title: A Demonstration in Tokyo
chapters.bigQuestion: How did an art from the Ryukyu Islands become a Japanese school subject and then a word on American signs?

story.title: An Empty Floor in Tokyo
story.kicker: In 1922 a schoolteacher from Okinawa shows Tokyo an art most people there have never seen.
paragraphs: It is the spring of 1922 in Tokyo, Japan. A national sports exhibition fills a hall. It is organized by Japan's Ministry of Education. Teachers from many parts of the country have come to show their subjects.

One visitor comes from far to the south. His name is Funakoshi Gichin. He is a schoolteacher from Shuri, on the island of Okinawa. He is in his early fifties. He has come to show an art his island calls karate.

Few people in Tokyo know the word. Okinawa had been its own kingdom, called Ryukyu, until 1879. Its arts grew there, with ideas carried by ships from China. Now Funakoshi stands before a Tokyo crowd with an empty floor in front of him.

People notice. Kanō Jigorō, the founder of judo, invites Funakoshi to show karate at his Kodokan school. Funakoshi was expected to go home. Instead he stays in Tokyo, teaching and writing, for the rest of his life.
story.think: Why might a teacher decide to stay far from home to teach an art to strangers?

lessons.title: The Ryukyu Kingdom
lessons.mainIdea: Karate began in the Ryukyu Kingdom, an island nation that became part of Japan only in 1879.
reading: The *Ryukyu* Islands are a long chain in the sea. They stretch south from Japan toward Taiwan. The biggest island is Okinawa. For centuries these islands had their own kings, their own court and their own languages.

The kings lived in a castle at *Shuri*, on Okinawa. Ryukyu sent ships to China with gifts for the Chinese emperor. Chinese ships and envoys came back. Ryukyu also traded with Japan, Korea and ports in Southeast Asia.

In 1609 soldiers from Satsuma, a domain in southern Japan, invaded Ryukyu. After that, Satsuma controlled much of the kingdom. In 1879 Japan ended the kingdom and made it Okinawa Prefecture. The last king was sent to Tokyo.

words.d: the island chain south of Japan that was once an independent kingdom; Okinawa is its largest island
the royal capital of the Ryukyu Kingdom, on Okinawa; today part of the city of Naha

lessons.title: Hand and China Hand
lessons.mainIdea: Okinawans had a local art called te, and they also learned from Chinese teachers and traders.
reading: Okinawans had an old unarmed art often called *te*. Te simply means hand. We have few written records of how it was taught. Most lessons passed quietly from one teacher to a few students.

Ryukyu had close ties with Fuzhou, a port city in China's Fujian province. Okinawan students, officials and traders spent time there. Some of them studied Chinese boxing arts. A village of Chinese families, called Kume, also lived near Naha on Okinawa.

Okinawans came to write the art with two Chinese characters. They meant Tang hand, or *China hand*. Tang was an old name for China. The characters could be read tōde or karate. The name itself showed where some of the ideas came from.

words.d: an Okinawan word meaning hand; an old name for local unarmed arts
the first meaning of the written word karate, from characters meaning Tang (China) hand
a port city in Fujian province, China, where many Okinawans traveled and studied

look.prompt: How could trips like this one change the arts taught back on Okinawa?

check.why: The first characters meant Tang hand, or China hand. Empty hand came later.

lessons.title: Teachers in Shuri and Naha
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, karate teachers in different Okinawan towns kept different lessons.
reading: Karate on Okinawa was not one school. Teachers in Shuri, Naha and the village of Tomari each had their own lessons. Later writers called these Shuri-te, Naha-te and Tomari-te. The names mean the hand of each town.
*Itosu Ankō* taught in Shuri. He lived from 1831 to 1915. He worked for the royal government before the kingdom ended. Funakoshi Gichin was one of his students.
*Higaonna Kanryō* taught in Naha. He lived from 1853 to 1915. As a young man he went to Fuzhou and studied there for years. His student Miyagi Chōjun later founded a style called Gōjū-ryū.

words.d: a karate teacher in Shuri (1831–1915) who taught Funakoshi Gichin
a karate teacher in Naha (1853–1915) who studied in Fuzhou, China

look.prompt: Why might two towns only a few miles apart keep different lessons?

lessons.title: Karate Goes to School
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1900s, karate entered Okinawa's schools as a subject for building fit students.
reading: After 1879 Okinawa followed Japan's school system. Japan wanted strong, healthy students and future soldiers. In the early 1900s, Itosu Ankō helped bring karate into Okinawan schools as *physical education*. This meant school lessons for the body.

Teaching a whole class was new. Old teachers had taught one or two students at a time. Itosu made simpler lessons that many children could learn in rows. He named a set of beginner *kata* Pinan. A kata is a fixed pattern practiced alone, like a written piece of music.

In 1908 Itosu wrote a letter with ten points about karate. It was meant for school officials. It said karate was for health and for building character, not for hurting people. Historians still read this letter as an early plan for karate in schools.

words.d: school lessons that build health and strength of the body
a set pattern of movements practiced alone; karate teachers name each one

look.title: Itosu's Ten Points, 1908
look.text: Karate is not learned only for oneself. It builds the body and a strong spirit. It is not meant to injure others. Taught in schools, it can help students become useful to their country.

check.q: What did Itosu's 1908 letter say karate was for?

lessons.title: Funakoshi in Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: Funakoshi Gichin's 1922 demonstration and book brought karate to mainland Japan.
reading: *Funakoshi Gichin* was born in Shuri in 1868. He became a schoolteacher. He studied karate with Itosu Ankō and with another Shuri teacher, Azato Ankō. He also wrote poems under the pen name Shōtō.

In 1922 Funakoshi showed karate at a *demonstration* in Tokyo. A demonstration is a public showing, not a contest. Kanō Jigorō then invited him to show karate at the Kodokan, the judo school. That same year Funakoshi published a book about karate.
Funakoshi stayed in Tokyo. He was poor at first and lived in a dormitory for Okinawan students. He taught students from universities and wrote more books. He died in Tokyo in 1957.

words.d: an Okinawan schoolteacher (1868–1957) who brought karate to Tokyo in 1922
a public showing of an art or skill, not a contest with a winner

look.text: A student in Tokyo buys a small new book in 1922. The title uses the old characters for China hand. Inside are drawings, a history of Okinawa and a list of kata names. The author is a teacher from Shuri.
look.prompt: Why would a printed book help an art travel farther than one teacher could?

lessons.title: China Hand Becomes Empty Hand
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1930s, karate's written name changed from China hand to empty hand.
reading: In the 1930s, Japan and China were moving toward war. The name China hand now sounded wrong to many people in Japan. Teachers looked for a new way to write karate.

They kept the sound karate but changed one character. The new characters meant *empty hand*. Funakoshi used the new writing in his 1935 book Karate-dō Kyōhan. He explained empty as a hand without a weapon, and also as a mind free of bad thoughts.
In 1936 senior karate teachers met in Naha, on Okinawa. They agreed to use the empty hand writing. They also added *dō*, which means way. Karate became karate-dō, the way of the empty hand.

words.d: the meaning of karate as written since the 1930s
a Japanese word meaning way or path, added to names like judo and karate-dō

look.prompt: Why might a teacher change how a word is written but keep how it sounds?

lessons.title: Universities and Styles
lessons.mainIdea: In mainland Japan, university clubs and named styles gave karate new rooms and ranks.
reading: In 1924 Keio University in Tokyo started a karate club. It is often named as the first university karate club in Japan. Funakoshi taught there. Other universities soon started clubs too.

Karate took ideas from judo. Clubs began to use a white uniform and colored belts. They also used *dan* ranks, the black belt levels that Kanō had created for judo. This made karate look like other Japanese school arts.

Different teachers named their own *styles*. A style is one teacher's line of lessons with its own name. Funakoshi's became known as Shotokan, from his pen name Shōtō. Miyagi Chōjun's was called Gōjū-ryū. Each style kept its own kata and its own ranks.

words.d: a black belt level; the system began in judo and spread to karate
a named line of karate lessons that goes back to one teacher

lessons.title: After 1945
lessons.mainIdea: After World War II, American service members learned karate in Okinawa and Japan and opened schools at home.
reading: World War II ended in 1945. The Battle of Okinawa that spring killed a huge number of people, many of them Okinawan civilians. After the war the United States ruled Okinawa. It returned Okinawa to Japan only in 1972.

Large American military bases stood on Okinawa. Some *service members* trained with Okinawan and Japanese karate teachers. When they went home, a few opened karate schools in the United States. Karate schools spread across American towns in the 1950s and 1960s.

In American *storefronts*, names began to blur. A sign might say karate over a room that taught a Korean or Chinese art. Many Americans used karate as a word for any art from East Asia. The teachers behind the signs came from many different lines.

words.d: people who serve in the armed forces, such as soldiers, sailors and Marines
a school or shop in a small street-level space, often with a sign in the window

lessons.title: Karate at the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Karate was an Olympic sport once, at the Tokyo Games held in 2021.
reading: Karate grew into a world sport with its own *federation*. A federation is a group that sets rules and runs contests. The World Karate Federation runs the Olympic kind of karate. It chose shared rules so that many styles could meet.

Karate joined the Olympic program for the Tokyo 2020 Games. The Games were delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and held in 2021. Karate had two kinds of events. In kata, judges scored a solo pattern. In kumite, two athletes faced each other under a points system.

The Olympic sport was chosen for Tokyo, not for every Games. Karate was not on the program for Paris 2024. Okinawa built the Okinawa Karate Kaikan, a center for karate history and training, which opened in 2017 in Tomigusuku.

words.d: a group that writes the rules and runs contests for a sport

chapters.title: A Korean School Sport
chapters.bigQuestion: How did South Korea build taekwondo into a national sport and then an Olympic one?

story.title: A Plan for Every School
story.kicker: After years of war and division, South Korea sets out to give one art one name and one plan.
paragraphs: It is the 1960s in Seoul, South Korea. The country is still rebuilding after the Korean War, which stopped in 1953. Many small schools teach unarmed arts. Each school is called a kwan, and each has its own name and teacher.
Leaders of the kwan meet in crowded offices. They argue about names, ranks and who should lead. Slowly they agree to join one national association. The art will have one name: taekwondo.
The association writes plans for ranks and lessons. The art is taught in the army, in schools and in clubs. A certificate from the national body now means the same thing in every city.
The goal grows bigger. Leaders want taekwondo known around the world as a Korean sport. That goal would lead, many years later, to an Olympic mat in Sydney, Australia.
story.think: Why might a country want one name and one plan for an art taught by many schools?

lessons.title: Old Korean Games
lessons.mainIdea: Korea had old arts such as ssireum wrestling and taekkyeon long before the name taekwondo.
reading: Korea has very old games of strength. Wall paintings in tombs of the Goguryeo kingdom show two men wrestling. Goguryeo ruled northern Korea and part of Manchuria about 1,500 years ago.

*Ssireum* is Korean wrestling. Pairs meet in a sand circle, and village festivals held ssireum matches for centuries. In 2018 UNESCO listed ssireum as cultural heritage. North and South Korea asked for it together.

*Taekkyeon* is an older Korean art with flowing, dance-like movement. Paintings and writings from the Joseon era show it as a game and contest. In 2011 UNESCO listed taekkyeon as cultural heritage of Korea.

words.d: traditional Korean wrestling, held in a sand circle at festivals
an old Korean art with flowing movement, listed by UNESCO in 2011
a United Nations group that lists and protects cultural heritage around the world

look.title: A Sand Circle at a Festival
look.text: It is a harvest festival in a Korean village long ago. A circle of sand is raked smooth. Two wrestlers wear cloth belts tied around the waist and thigh. Families watch from the edge. The winner may take home a bull as a prize.
look.prompt: What does this scene tell you about ssireum's place in village life?

check.why: Ssireum is traditional Korean wrestling, held in a sand circle.

check.why: UNESCO listed taekkyeon as cultural heritage in 2011.

check.q: What do Goguryeo tomb paintings show?
check.why: Goguryeo tomb paintings show wrestlers, proof of very old Korean games of strength.

lessons.title: Years of Colonial Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Japan ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945, and some Koreans learned Japanese arts such as karate in those years.
reading: In 1910 Japan took over Korea and made it a *colony*. A colony is a land ruled by another country. Japan ruled Korea for 35 years. Korean schools had to teach in Japanese, and Korean customs were pushed aside.

Judo and kendo were taught in Korean schools and police training under Japanese rule. Some Korean young men went to Japan to study at universities. There, a few joined karate clubs and trained for years.
Japan's rule ended in 1945, when Japan lost World War II. Koreans call that day *liberation*. The Korean men who had learned karate came home. They would soon open schools of their own.

words.d: a land ruled by another country
the end of Japanese rule over Korea in 1945

look.prompt: What might this student keep from his training, and what might he want to change?

lessons.title: The First Kwan
lessons.mainIdea: After 1945, Korean teachers opened schools called kwan that taught karate-based lessons.
reading: After liberation, several new schools opened, mostly in Seoul. Each was called a *kwan*, a Korean word for a hall or school. Chung Do Kwan and Moo Duk Kwan were two of the best known.

Most kwan taught lessons based on the karate their founders had learned. They used Korean names for it. Some called it tang soo do, the Korean reading of China hand. Others called it kong soo do, the Korean reading of empty hand.
The Korean War began in 1950 and stopped in 1953. Fighting divided the country and destroyed much of Seoul. When the kwan reopened, many of their teachers had served in the South Korean army.

words.d: a Korean word for a hall or school; the early schools of taekwondo were each a kwan
the Korean reading of the characters for China hand, an early name used by some kwan

look.title: Two Readings of One Word
look.text: In Japanese, the old characters read karate, meaning China hand. In Korean, the same characters read tang soo do. The newer Japanese writing meant empty hand. In Korean, that one read kong soo do.
look.prompt: What does this tell you about where the first kwan got their lessons?

check.why: Kwan is a Korean word for a hall or school.

check.q: What did tang soo do mean?
check.why: Tang soo do is the Korean reading of the characters for China hand.

check.q: When did the Korean War stop?
check.why: The Korean War began in 1950 and stopped in 1953.

lessons.title: Naming Taekwondo
lessons.mainIdea: In 1955 the name taekwondo was chosen, meaning roughly the way of foot and fist.
reading: In 1955 a group of teachers and leaders met in Seoul to pick a new name. They chose *taekwondo*. General Choi Hong-hi, an army officer who ran a kwan, is often named as the one who proposed it.
The name has three parts. Tae means foot or to kick. Kwon means fist or hand. Do means way, the same word as the Japanese dō. Together it means roughly the way of foot and fist.
The new name sounded like taekkyeon, the older Korean art. That was on purpose, many historians say. Leaders wanted a name that pointed to Korea, not Japan. Not every kwan used the new name at first.

words.d: a Korean martial art and sport; the name means roughly the way of foot and fist
a South Korean army general often named as the one who proposed the name taekwondo

look.title: Three Parts of a Name

lessons.title: A National Association
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1960s, many kwan joined one national association, and the art spread through the army and schools.
reading: In the early 1960s, South Korea's government pushed the kwan to unite. They formed one national *association*. It changed its name more than once. By 1965 it was called the Korea Taekwondo Association.

The association set shared ranks and tests. The South Korean army trained soldiers in taekwondo. Korean instructors went abroad too, including to Vietnam, where South Korean troops served in the 1960s.

Not everyone agreed about who should lead. In 1966 Choi Hong-hi founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation in Seoul. Later it moved its headquarters out of South Korea. Two taekwondo bodies, with different rules and forms, still exist today.

words.d: an organized group that joins many schools and sets shared rules
a taekwondo body founded by Choi Hong-hi in 1966; it has its own rules and forms

lessons.title: Kukkiwon and World Taekwondo
lessons.mainIdea: Kukkiwon in Seoul became taekwondo's national headquarters, and World Taekwondo runs the sport worldwide.
reading: In 1972 *Kukkiwon* opened in Seoul. Its name means national hall. It is the headquarters of taekwondo in South Korea. Kukkiwon gives out dan certificates, the papers that record black belt ranks, to students around the world.

In 1973 the World Taekwondo Federation was founded in Seoul. It set rules for contests between countries. In 2017 it shortened its name to *World Taekwondo*. It runs world championships and the Olympic events.

Kukkiwon also set new forms in the early 1970s. They were named Taegeuk, after the red and blue circle on South Korea's flag. They replaced older forms borrowed from karate. In 2018 South Korea passed a law naming taekwondo its national martial art.

lessons.title: From Demonstration to Medals
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo was shown at the 1988 and 1992 Olympics and became a full medal sport in 2000.
reading: Seoul hosted the Summer Olympics in 1988. Taekwondo appeared there as a *demonstration sport*. That meant it was shown at the Games, but its medals did not count. It was shown again in Barcelona, Spain, in 1992.

In 2000 the Olympics came to Sydney, Australia. Taekwondo became a full *medal sport* there. Men and women each had four weight classes. That made eight events, with the same number for women and men from the start.
Many countries won medals, not only Korea. This showed how far the sport had spread. Taekwondo has been on the Olympic program at every Summer Games since Sydney.

words.d: a sport shown at the Olympics whose medals do not count in the official record

lessons.title: New Rules for a Watched Sport
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic taekwondo added electronic scoring and Paralympic events as the sport grew.
reading: Early contests were scored by judges pressing buttons. Fans and coaches often argued about the scores. World Taekwondo brought in *electronic scoring*, with sensors in the body protectors. The London 2012 Olympics used this system.

Olympic contests use a set *weight class*, a round clock and a square or eight-sided mat. These rules let athletes from any country meet on fair terms. The rules also reward some scoring moves with more points than others.

Doors opened for more athletes. Para taekwondo, for athletes with impairments of the arms, joined the Paralympic Games in Tokyo. Those Games were held in 2021. Refugee athletes have also competed under a refugee team flag.

words.d: a system that counts points with sensors in the athletes' protective gear

lessons.title: More Than Korean Karate
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo began with karate lessons but was rebuilt with a Korean name, forms, rules and national bodies.
reading: Some people call taekwondo Korean karate. There is a true part to this, because taekwondo has karate *roots*. The first kwan teachers had trained in Japanese karate. Their early forms and belts came from karate.

But taekwondo leaders changed much after 1955. They chose a Korean name and built national bodies. Kukkiwon wrote new Taegeuk forms. World Taekwondo wrote contest rules that are different from karate's rules.

Leaders also made taekwondo a *national symbol* and tied taekwondo to older Korean arts such as taekkyeon. Historians still debate how close that tie is. Today taekwondo is taught in more than 200 countries, many of which belong to World Taekwondo.

words.d: where an art first came from, such as the karate learned by the first kwan teachers
